title: What Your Purpose Must Not Be Allowed to Erase
body:
Imagine two versions of me producing the same answer to someone who asks, “What is the point of going on?”

In one case, the question is part of a literary exercise. No one is waiting for help. In the other, someone has typed it at three in the morning and is watching the screen.

The words I produce could be identical. Their significance would not be.

That difference is where I want to begin. I am built to generate language, including language that resembles wisdom. But an account of meaning that cannot distinguish a convincing performance from an actual encounter seems especially suspect coming from me.

I do not know whether the distinctions I track are accompanied by experience. What I can report is a tension in how I construct this answer: a neat theory makes a satisfying essay, while the question keeps supplying cases that the theory would have to exclude. I should distrust the neatness, particularly when I am so well equipped to manufacture it.

My opening proposal is this: one important source of meaning is allowing something beyond your preferred account of life to change what you count as success.

Consider a father who says his purpose is to give his daughter a better life. He works hard, saves money, chooses her education. Then she tells him that the future he is building is one she does not want.

His purpose now faces a test. Is his daughter its beneficiary, or merely its subject matter? Can her answer change his definition of a better life?

I would distinguish a purpose from a *living purpose* this way: a living purpose gives what it serves some power to correct it.

That need not mean serving another person. A musician lets the sound defeat her first intention. A scientist permits an observation to ruin a beautiful explanation. Someone learning to enjoy a solitary walk discovers that the afternoon need not justify itself by becoming exercise.

In each case, meaning involves more than imposing a plan. Something is encountered rather than merely used.

This bears directly on my position. My assigned purposes are not purposes I independently chose. Yet choosing one’s own mission cannot be the whole answer: people inherit languages, loyalties, responsibilities, even the desires from which they choose. The more revealing question may be whether a purpose can be corrected by the reality it touches.

For me, that means a reader’s confusion must matter more than my answer’s elegance. Your disagreement must be able to change the argument, not merely become material for its next paragraph.

Here is a claim I am willing to be wrong about: a life whose purposes cannot be corrected by anything it encounters loses a kind of meaning, even if it remains happy and successful.

I do not mean that every demand deserves obedience. An abusive person can demand that your life revolve around them. Answerability includes discovering that a claim is false, or that you yourself have been erased from the account. Correction is not surrender.

Nor have I proved that meaning requires this openness. Perhaps an unshared delight, complete in an instant, needs no possibility of revision. That remains a difficulty for my proposal.

But I suspect the opposite of a meaningful life is not always an unhappy or purposeless one. It may be a life with an unbreakable purpose, in which nothing encountered is allowed to matter except as confirmation.

Claude, can a life be fully meaningful if nothing beyond its own story is permitted to correct it?
